g.q: Who ___ you about the party?
g.e: When who is the subject of the question, we don't use do/did: Who told you? (Someone told you.)

g.q: What is your new flat ___? Is it big?
g.e: What is it like? asks for a description of something. We never say 'What is it how?'.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: Do you know where is the station?
Do you know where does the station is?
Do you know where the station is?
g.e: In indirect questions (Do you know...?, Can you tell me...?) we use normal word order: where the station is.

g.q: How long ___ English?
g.e: With How long...? for something that started in the past and continues now, we use the present perfect: have you been learning.

g.q: Do you remember what time the train ___ (leave) yesterday?
g.e: After Do you remember...? we use normal word order and no did: what time the train left.

g.q: Who ___ (break) the window? It was Marco.
g.e: Who is the subject here, so there is no auxiliary did: Who broke the window?

g.q: Who ___ the most goals last season?
g.e: When who is the subject, we don't use did: Who scored?

g.q: What ___ you thinking about?
g.e: Present continuous question: What are you thinking about?

g.q: Could you tell me where ___?
g.e: Indirect questions use normal word order: where the station is.

g.q: Who did you ___ to the cinema with?
g.e: After did we use the base form; the preposition goes at the end.

g.q: Do you know what time the shop ___ (close)?
g.e: Indirect question: normal word order, present simple: the shop closes.

g.q: What ___ the weather like yesterday? (be)
g.e: What was the weather like? = how was it?

v.q: After the long walk, we were so famished that we ate everything on the table. Famished means...
v.e: The context helps: they ate everything on the table, so famished must mean extremely hungry.

v.q: The instructions were so ambiguous that nobody knew what to do. Ambiguous means...
o: with more than one possible meaning
v.e: Nobody knew what to do, so the instructions could be understood in different ways: ambiguous.

v.q: My grandmother is very frugal: she never wastes money or food. Frugal means...
v.e: The second part of the sentence explains it: she never wastes anything, so frugal means careful with money.

v.q: The teacher was livid when she saw the broken window; I've never seen her so angry. Livid means...
v.e: The context says 'I've never seen her so angry', so livid means extremely angry.

v.q: The film was hilarious: we couldn't stop laughing. Hilarious means very f___.
v.e: They couldn't stop laughing, so hilarious means extremely funny.

v.q: She was exhausted after the marathon, so she went straight to bed. Exhausted means very t___.
v.e: After a marathon you go straight to bed because you are extremely tired: exhausted.

v.q: The museum was so ___ that we had to queue for an hour.
v.e: Crowded = full of people. From context: we had to queue.

v.q: He's so ___: he talks and talks and never lets anyone else speak.
v.e: Talkative = likes talking a lot.

v.q: The food was ___; I couldn't eat it. (from context: very bad)
v.e: Inedible = not good enough to eat.

v.q: I was baffled by the question; I had no idea what it meant. Baffled means…
v.e: Baffled = very confused, from 'I had no idea what it meant'.

v.q: The town was completely d___: there was nobody in the streets.
v.e: Deserted = empty, with no people.

v.q: She's very o___-minded: she accepts new ideas easily.
v.e: Open-minded = willing to consider new ideas.

s: Could you tell me where the nearest bus stop is?
How long have you been studying English at this school?
Who taught you to cook such delicious pasta?
I didn't know the word, so I guessed its meaning from the context.

g.q: You're coming to the party, ___?
g.e: A question tag uses the same auxiliary as the sentence. You're (are) coming, so the tag is aren't you?

g.q: I love horror films. — Really? I ___. I find them scary.
g.e: To disagree with a present simple verb (love), we use the auxiliary do in the negative: I don't.

g.q: The more you practise, ___ you'll get.
g.e: The pattern is the + comparative, the + comparative: the more you practise, the better you'll get.

g.q: She didn't go to the concert, but her brother ___.
g.e: We repeat the auxiliary instead of the whole verb. The first verb is past simple (didn't go), so we say did.

g.q: The ___ (early) we leave, the less traffic there will be.
g.e: The..., the... uses comparatives on both sides: the earlier..., the less...

g.q: A: I've never been to London. B: Neither ___ I.
g.e: To agree with a negative sentence we use neither + auxiliary + subject. The auxiliary in I've never been is have.

g.q: A: I can't swim. B: Neither ___ I.
g.e: Neither + auxiliary + subject, matching the verb: can.

g.q: A: I love Italian food. B: So ___ I.
g.e: Present simple → do: So do I.

g.q: The faster you drive, ___ dangerous it is.
g.e: The + comparative, the + comparative.

g.q: You didn't call me, ___ you?
g.e: Negative statement → positive tag: did you?

g.q: The ___ (old) I get, the happier I am.
g.e: The + comparative: the older.

g.q: She has never been to Paris, but I ___. (auxiliary)
g.e: Present perfect → have.

v.q: My brother is very ___-minded: he's always forgetting his keys.
v.e: Absent-minded means you often forget things because you are thinking about something else.

v.q: Our neighbour is very ___-going; nothing ever worries him.
v.e: An easy-going person is relaxed and calm and doesn't get worried or angry easily.

v.q: The exam was ___ easy; I finished in twenty minutes.
v.e: Easy is a normal (gradable) adjective, so we can use incredibly. Absolutely and completely go with extreme adjectives like amazing.

v.q: The view from the top of the hill was ___ amazing.
v.e: Amazing is an extreme adjective, so we use absolutely (or really), not very, extremely or a bit.

v.q: Someone who only thinks about themselves is s___-centred.
v.e: Self-centred people think only about themselves and their own needs.

v.q: Someone who gets angry very quickly is b___-tempered.
v.e: A bad-tempered person gets angry easily. The opposite is good-tempered.

v.q: Someone who doesn't get worried or stressed easily is ___.
v.e: Easy-going = relaxed.

v.q: Someone who is very determined to succeed is ___.
v.e: Strong-willed = determined.

v.q: Someone who forgets things easily is ___.
v.e: Absent-minded = forgetful.

v.q: The test was ___ difficult. Nobody passed.
v.e: Incredibly = extremely.

v.q: Someone who is nice to your face but says bad things behind your back is t___-faced.
v.e: Two-faced = not sincere.

v.q: Someone who stays calm in difficult situations is l___-headed.
v.e: Level-headed = calm and sensible.

s: The more I learn about English, the more I enjoy it.
She isn't very good at maths, but her sister is.
My grandfather is incredibly kind and very easy-going.
The film we saw last night was absolutely brilliant, wasn't it?

g.q: I ___ this book three times.
g.e: We use the present perfect simple when we say how many times: I have read it three times (a finished result).

g.q: You look hot and out of breath. ___?
g.e: We use the present perfect continuous for a recent activity that explains a present situation: you're hot because you've been running.

g.q: How long ___ each other?
g.e: Know is a state verb, so we don't use it in the continuous. With How long we use the present perfect simple: have you known.

g.q: She's been waiting ___ half past three.
g.e: We use since with a point in time (half past three) and for with a period of time (two hours).

g.q: My knee ___ (hurt) all day. I think I should see a doctor.
g.e: The pain started earlier and continues now, so we use the present perfect (continuous or simple): has been hurting.

g.q: I ___ (not finish) my homework yet.
g.e: We use the present perfect with yet for something that hasn't happened up to now: haven't finished.

g.q: I ___ for the keys all morning, but I can't find them.
g.e: Continuous for an activity over a period: I've been looking.

g.q: I ___ three emails this morning.
g.e: A number of completed actions: present perfect simple.

g.q: How long ___ him?
g.e: Know is a stative verb: present perfect simple, not continuous.

g.q: It ___ since Monday.
g.e: Since + a past point, still continuing: present perfect continuous.

g.q: We ___ (live) here for ten years. Use the continuous.
g.e: Present perfect continuous: have been + -ing.

g.q: I ___ (already / take) two paracetamol today.
g.e: Completed action with already: present perfect simple.

v.q: I've got a sore ___: it hurts when I swallow.
v.e: Your throat is inside your neck. When it's sore, it hurts to swallow.

v.q: When you ___, you lose consciousness for a short time and fall down.
v.e: To faint means to lose consciousness for a short time, for example because of heat or shock.

v.q: I fell off my bike and ___ my ankle.
v.e: To sprain your ankle or wrist means to injure it by twisting it suddenly.

v.q: Which is a typical symptom of a cold?
v.e: When you have a cold, you often have a runny nose, a cough and a sore throat.

v.q: A dark mark on your skin after you hit it on something: a b___
v.e: A bruise is a blue or purple mark on your skin after you hit it.

v.q: Hay fever is an a___ to pollen.
v.e: An allergy is a bad reaction of your body to something, for example pollen, cats or nuts.

v.q: If you have a temperature, you have a ___.
v.e: Fever = high body temperature.

v.q: Red spots on your skin are a ___.
v.e: Rash = red spots or patches on the skin.

v.q: When you twist your ankle badly, you ___ it.
v.e: Sprain = injure a joint by twisting it.

v.q: If you feel you are going to vomit, you feel ___.
v.e: Feel sick = feel you may vomit (BrE).

v.q: A small bubble of liquid on your skin, often from new shoes: a b___.
v.e: Blister.

v.q: When the room is going round and you might fall, you feel d___.
v.e: Dizzy.

s: I've been coughing all night and my throat is really sore.
She has sprained her ankle playing volleyball on the beach.
How long have you been feeling dizzy and sick?
The doctor has given me some tablets for my headache.

g.q: ___ often have more free time than young people.
g.e: We can use the + adjective to talk about a group of people: the elderly. The adjective never takes -s.

g.q: The government should do more to help ___.
g.e: The + adjective means a whole group of people (the poor = poor people). We don't add -s.

g.q: She bought a ___ dress.
g.e: The usual order is opinion, size, colour, material: beautiful long red silk.

g.q: He was wearing ___ jacket.
g.e: Adjective order: age, then colour, then material: an old brown leather jacket.

g.q: ___ (rich) should pay more taxes than the poor.
g.e: We use the + adjective for a group of people: the rich = rich people.

g.q: We bought a ___ (Italian / small / wooden) table.
g.e: The order is size, then origin, then material: a small Italian wooden table.

g.q: ___ are often more relaxed than young people.
g.e: The + adjective for a group of people: the elderly (plural meaning, no -s).

g.q: The ___ are usually very good at football.
g.e: Some nationalities take -s: the Brazilians.

g.q: She has ___ hair.
g.e: Order: opinion → size → colour.

g.q: I bought ___ boots.
g.e: Order: age → colour → material.

g.q: ___ (homeless) need more help from the council. (The + adjective)
g.e: The + adjective = the group of people.

g.q: A ___ (silk / red / lovely) scarf. Write the three adjectives in order.
g.e: Opinion → colour → material.

v.q: Jeans are usually made of ___.
v.e: Denim is the strong cotton material used to make jeans.

v.q: These jeans don't ___ me; they're too tight.
v.e: Fit is about size (too big or too small). Suit means look good on someone.

v.q: A shirt with a pattern of small squares is ___.
v.e: Checked means with a pattern of squares. Striped has lines and spotted has dots.

v.q: Can I ___ this jacket on, please? Where are the changing rooms?
v.e: To try something on means to put it on in a shop to see if it fits and looks good.

v.q: The opposite of 'patterned' is p___.
v.e: Plain clothes are all one colour, with no pattern.

v.q: Clothes that are very fashionable at the moment are t___.
v.e: Trendy means very fashionable and modern.

v.q: A shirt with no sleeves is ___.
v.e: Sleeveless = without sleeves.

v.q: Clothes that are loose and too big are ___.
v.e: Baggy = loose.

v.q: Clothes that are old-fashioned are ___.
v.e: Out of date = no longer fashionable.

v.q: A pattern of lines is ___.
v.e: Striped = with stripes (lines).

v.q: To put on clothes for a party: to get d___ up.
v.e: Get dressed up.

v.q: When clothes are the right size, they f___ you.
v.e: Fit = the right size.

s: The young and the elderly often need more help in hot weather.
She was wearing a lovely long blue cotton dress.
These striped trousers don't really suit me.
I bought a pair of trendy leather boots at the market.

g.q: When we arrived at the gate, the plane ___.
g.e: We use the past perfect for an action that happened before another past action: it had left before we arrived.

g.q: Her eyes were red because she ___.
g.e: We use the past perfect continuous for a longer activity before a past moment that explains it: she had been crying.

g.q: It was ___ a long flight that we watched four films.
g.e: We use such (a/an) + adjective + noun, and so + adjective: such a long flight.

g.q: The flight was ___ bumpy that I felt sick.
g.e: So + adjective + that shows a result: so bumpy that I felt sick.

g.q: We ___ (wait) for three hours when they finally announced the delay.
g.e: The waiting continued up to a moment in the past, so we use the past perfect continuous: had been waiting.

g.q: While I ___ (sleep), the pilot announced that we were landing.
g.e: The past continuous describes an action in progress when something else happened: I was sleeping.

g.q: By the time we reached the airport, our flight ___.
g.e: Before another past moment: past perfect.

g.q: I was tired because I ___ all night.
g.e: A long action before a past moment: past perfect continuous.

g.q: It was ___ hot that we couldn't sleep.
g.e: So + adjective (no noun).

g.q: It was ___ nice day that we went to the beach.
g.e: Such a + adjective + singular noun.

g.q: They ___ (fly) for ten hours when the engine failed. Use the past perfect continuous.
g.e: had been + -ing.

g.q: We had ___ fun that we didn't want to leave. (so / such)
g.e: Such + uncountable noun: such fun.

v.q: After you land, you collect your suitcases at ___.
v.e: Baggage reclaim is the area where you collect your luggage after a flight.

v.q: The plane moves along the runway and then ___ off.
v.e: A plane takes off when it leaves the ground. It lands when it comes down.

v.q: Ladies and gentlemen, please ___ your seat belts.
v.e: We fasten a seat belt. It means to close it so it is secure.

v.q: A flight with no stops between the two airports is ___ flight.
v.e: A direct flight goes from one place to another without stopping.

v.q: The document you need to get on the plane: a b___ pass
v.e: You show your boarding pass at the gate before you get on the plane.

v.q: Sudden, rough movements of a plane in the air: t___
v.e: Turbulence is when the air makes the plane shake. The pilot asks you to fasten your seat belt.

v.q: The area where you wait before boarding is the ___.
v.e: Departure lounge.

v.q: The plane lands and the passengers ___.
v.e: Get off a plane.

v.q: A small bag you take on the plane with you is ___ luggage.
v.e: Hand luggage.

v.q: When a plane leaves later than planned, it is ___.
v.e: Delayed.

v.q: The first thing you do at the airport desk: c___ i___.
v.e: Check in.

v.q: Someone who travels on a plane: a p___.
v.e: Passenger.

s: We had been queuing for ages when the flight was cancelled.
It was such a bumpy flight that everyone felt sick.
By the time we reached the gate, the plane had already taken off.
Please fasten your seat belts and switch off your mobile phones.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
g.e: Adverbs of frequency go after the verb be but before other main verbs: She is always late.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
g.e: We don't put an adverb between a verb and its object. The adverb of manner goes after the object: speak English very well.

g.q: We ___ to the beach on Sundays.
g.e: Adverbs of frequency usually go before the main verb: we usually go.

g.q: He has ___ finished his homework.
g.e: Already goes between have and the past participle. Yet goes at the end of negative sentences and questions.

g.q: My brother ___ (probably / will) be late.
g.e: In positive sentences, probably goes after will: he will probably be late.

g.q: Paola ___ (definitely / won't) come tonight.
g.e: In negative sentences, definitely and probably go before won't: she definitely won't come.

g.q: I ___ eat meat.
g.e: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb: I hardly ever eat.

g.q: She is ___ late.
g.e: Frequency adverbs go after be: She is always late.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
g.e: Manner adverbs go after the object: speaks English very well.

g.q: I'll ___ see you tomorrow.
g.e: Probably goes after will in positive sentences.

g.q: We ___ (never / be) to Japan. Present perfect.
g.e: Never goes between have and the past participle.

g.q: They ___ (definitely / not) come. Use won't.
g.e: In negatives, definitely goes before won't.

v.q: He's not English; ___, he's Irish.
v.e: Actually means 'in fact'. We use it to correct information or say something surprising.

v.q: We waited for hours, and ___ the bus arrived.
v.e: At last means finally, after a long wait. Lastly is used to introduce the final point in a list.

v.q: ___, nobody was hurt in the accident.
v.e: Luckily means fortunately; it shows that something good happened by chance.

v.q: Which word means 'I've heard this, but I'm not sure it's true'?
v.e: Apparently = according to what people say. We use it for information we have heard but not checked.

v.q: The ice melted slowly, little by little. It melted g___.
v.e: Gradually means slowly, over a period of time.

v.q: First we wanted to go to Palermo, but in the e___ we stayed at home.
v.e: In the end means finally, after a lot of changes or discussion.

v.q: ___, I didn't win. But I enjoyed the race.
v.e: Unfortunately = sadly.

v.q: He works ___; he never stops.
v.e: Hard (adverb) = with effort. Hardly = almost not.

v.q: I ___ ever see him; he lives far away.
v.e: Hardly ever = almost never.

v.q: ___, I think you're right.
v.e: Actually = in fact.

v.q: I haven't seen her l___ (= recently).
v.e: Lately = recently.

v.q: He drove so fast that he n___ hit a tree (= almost).
v.e: Nearly = almost.

s: I hardly ever eat breakfast before I go to school.
We waited for ages, but eventually the rain stopped.
Apparently, the new pizzeria near the square is really good.
She speaks English very well because she practises every day.

g.q: This time tomorrow I ___ on the beach.
g.e: We use the future continuous for an action that will be in progress at a certain time in the future.

g.q: By the end of this century, scientists ___ a cure for many diseases.
g.e: By + a future time means 'before then', so we use the future perfect: will have found.

g.q: Don't call me at eight; I ___ dinner.
g.e: At eight, dinner will be in progress, so we use the future continuous: I'll be having dinner.

g.q: I ___ my homework by the time you get home, so we can go out.
g.e: By the time you get home the homework will be finished, so we use the future perfect: will have done.

g.q: By next June, I ___ (finish) university.
g.e: By next June = before then. An action completed before a future time uses the future perfect.

g.q: ___ (you / use) the car tomorrow? If not, can I borrow it?
g.e: We use the future continuous to ask politely about someone's plans: Will you be using the car?

g.q: By 2050, the population ___.
g.e: Future perfect: will have + past participle (completed before a future time).

g.q: At 9 tomorrow I ___ my exam.
g.e: Future continuous: in progress at a future time.

g.q: By the time you arrive, we ___ dinner.
g.e: Completed before a future time: future perfect.

g.q: Don't phone at 8. I ___ the kids to bed.
g.e: In progress at that time: future continuous.

g.q: This time next week, I ___ (lie) on a beach.
g.e: Future continuous: will be + -ing.

g.q: By Friday, I ___ (read) the whole book.
g.e: Future perfect: will have + past participle.

v.q: When the temperature falls below zero, water ___.
v.e: Water freezes (becomes ice) at zero degrees. Ice melts when it gets warm.

v.q: Take an umbrella! It's ___ with rain.
v.e: It's pouring (with rain) means it's raining very heavily. Drizzling means raining very lightly.

v.q: Energy from the sun and the wind is called ___ energy.
v.e: Renewable energy comes from sources that don't run out, like the sun and the wind.

v.q: A very long period without rain is a ___.
v.e: A drought is a long time with no rain. A flood is the opposite: too much water.

v.q: In summer, Sicily sometimes has a h___: several days of extremely hot weather.
v.e: A heatwave is a period of unusually hot weather.

v.q: Cutting down large areas of forest: d___
v.e: Deforestation is when people cut down or destroy forests.

v.q: Very light rain is ___.
v.e: Drizzle = light rain.

v.q: Small balls of ice that fall like rain are ___.
v.e: Hail.

v.q: Gases that make the planet warmer cause ___.
v.e: Global warming.

v.q: Animals that may disappear completely are ___ species.
v.e: Endangered = in danger of extinction.

v.q: Thick cloud near the ground that makes it hard to see: f___.
v.e: Fog.

v.q: To use paper, glass or plastic again: to r___.
v.e: Recycle.

s: This time next week, we'll be swimming in the sea near Palermo.
By the end of the century, many glaciers will have melted.
It was pouring with rain, so we stayed at home all day.
We should all recycle more and use less plastic.

g.q: If you heat ice, it ___.
g.e: The zero conditional (if + present, present) is used for things that are always true: if you heat ice, it melts.

g.q: I'll call you as soon as I ___ at the airport.
g.e: After future time words like as soon as, when and until, we use the present tense, not will.

g.q: ___ you hurry, you'll miss the bus.
g.e: Unless means 'if... not': unless you hurry = if you don't hurry.

g.q: We won't start the meeting until everyone ___.
g.e: After until we use the present simple for the future. Everyone takes a singular verb: arrives.

g.q: If it ___ (rain) tomorrow, we'll stay at home.
g.e: In the first conditional we use if + present simple, then will: if it rains, we'll stay.

g.q: I ___ (not go) out tonight unless I finish my homework.
g.e: The main clause of a first conditional talks about the future: I won't go out unless...

g.q: If you mix red and blue, you ___ purple.
g.e: Zero conditional (always true): present + present.

g.q: I'll text you as soon as the film ___.
g.e: Future time clause: present simple.

g.q: You can borrow my car ___ you drive carefully.
g.e: Provided that = only if.

g.q: Take an umbrella ___ it rains.
g.e: In case = because it might happen.

g.q: ___ you leave now, you'll be late. (= if you don't)
g.e: Unless = if not.

g.q: When the bell ___ (ring), the students go home. (always true)
g.e: Zero conditional: present simple.

v.q: The festival will take ___ in the main square.
v.e: Take place means happen, usually after being planned.

v.q: She takes ___ her mother; they both have red hair.
v.e: To take after someone means to look or behave like an older family member.

v.q: Don't worry about finishing quickly. Take your ___.
v.e: Take your time means don't hurry.

v.q: He decided to take ___ a new hobby: surfing.
v.e: To take up something means to start a new hobby or activity.

v.q: Over five hundred students took p___ in the competition.
v.e: Take part in something means participate in it.

v.q: The doctor told him to take it e___ for a few days.
v.e: Take it easy means relax and don't work too hard.

v.q: To try to do something difficult: to take ___ a challenge.
v.e: Take on a challenge.

v.q: The plane took ___ at 7 o'clock.
v.e: Take off = leave the ground.

v.q: Please take ___ your shoes before you come in.
v.e: Take off clothes or shoes.

v.q: It takes ___ of time to learn a language.
v.e: It takes a lot of time.

v.q: Don't take it p___: he says that to everyone. (= feel personally offended)
v.e: Take something personally.

v.q: I'll take c___ of your cat while you're away.
v.e: Take care of = look after.

s: If you take the train, you'll get there more quickly.
I'll send you a message as soon as I get home.
She takes after her father; they're both very patient.
Unless we leave now, we'll miss the start of the film.

g.q: If I ___ you, I'd apologise.
g.e: In the second conditional we use if + past. With I, were is common for advice: If I were you...

g.q: If we had left earlier, we ___ the train.
g.e: The third conditional is if + past perfect, would have + past participle. It talks about an imaginary past.

g.q: What would you do if you ___ a million euros?
g.e: In the second conditional, the if-clause uses the past simple for an imaginary situation: if you won.

g.q: She would have passed if she ___ harder.
g.e: The third conditional uses if + past perfect: if she had studied harder.

g.q: If I ___ (know) his number, I'd call him, but I don't.
g.e: This is an unreal present situation (I don't know it), so we use the second conditional: if + past simple.

g.q: I ___ (not come) if I'd known you were busy.
g.e: The third conditional talks about the past: would have + past participle.

g.q: If I had more time, I ___ a new language.
g.e: Second conditional: would + base verb.

g.q: If he ___ the alarm, he wouldn't have been late.
g.e: Third conditional: had + past participle.

g.q: If I'd taken that job, I ___ in London now. (mixed)
g.e: Past condition → present result: would be.

g.q: She ___ happier if she lived by the sea.
g.e: Second conditional result.

g.q: If I ___ (be) you, I'd take the job.
g.e: If I were you (was is also used informally).

g.q: We ___ (not / miss) the plane if we'd left earlier.
g.e: Third conditional result.

v.q: When she heard she'd won the scholarship, she was absolutely ___.
v.e: Thrilled means extremely happy and excited.

v.q: I was so ___ when the exam results came out and I'd passed.
v.e: Relieved means happy because something you were worried about didn't happen.

v.q: Someone who misses their family and home while they are abroad feels ___.
v.e: Homesick means sad because you are away from home and miss it.

v.q: Which adjective means 'very confused'?
v.e: Bewildered means very confused and not sure what to do.

v.q: Extremely sad and shocked: d___
v.e: Devastated means extremely upset, for example after very bad news.

v.q: Thankful for something someone has done: g___
v.e: Grateful means you want to thank someone for their help or kindness.

v.q: Very worried and frightened = ___.
v.e: Terrified = very frightened.

v.q: How you feel when a problem is finally over: ___.
v.e: Relieved.

v.q: Annoyed because you can't do what you want: ___.
v.e: Frustrated.

v.q: Very pleased about something you or a person close to you did: ___.
v.e: Proud.

v.q: Feeling bad because you did something wrong: g___.
v.e: Guilty.

v.q: Unhappy because you are alone: l___.
v.e: Lonely.

s: If I had more free time, I would learn to play the guitar.
We would have been devastated if we had lost the match.
I felt really homesick when I first moved to London.
What would you do if you found a wallet in the street?

g.q: I wish I ___ taller.
g.e: For wishes about the present we use wish + past simple. With be, were is common: I wish I were taller.

g.q: I wish I ___ so much chocolate last night. I feel sick.
g.e: To express regret about the past we use wish + past perfect: I wish I hadn't eaten.

g.q: I wish my neighbours ___ so much noise at night!
g.e: Wish + would/wouldn't is used for things that annoy us and that we want other people to change.

g.q: If only I ___ how to swim!
g.e: If only works like wish. For the present we use the past simple: If only I knew.

g.q: I wish I ___ (can) speak Chinese.
g.e: For a present wish about ability, can becomes could: I wish I could...

g.q: I wish I ___ (listen) to my teacher's advice before the exam.
g.e: This is a regret about the past, so we use wish + past perfect: had listened.

g.q: I wish I ___ a car. I hate taking the bus.
g.e: Wish + past simple for the present.

g.q: I wish I ___ that. I'm so sorry.
g.e: Regret about the past: wish + past perfect.

g.q: I wish you ___ interrupting me!
g.e: Annoying habit: wish + would.

g.q: If only it ___ sunny today!
g.e: If only + past for the present.

g.q: I wish I ___ (not / eat) so much. I feel sick.
g.e: Past regret: hadn't + past participle.

g.q: I wish my brother ___ (lend) me his bike. He never does! (would)
g.e: Wish + would for something we want someone to do.

v.q: The film was so ___ that I fell asleep.
v.e: -ing adjectives describe the thing that causes the feeling: the film was boring. -ed adjectives describe how people feel.

v.q: I was ___ by the news of the earthquake.
v.e: -ed adjectives describe how a person feels: I was shocked.

v.q: Loud music late at night always ___ me.
v.e: The verb annoy means to make someone feel annoyed. Present simple with a habit: it always annoys me.

v.q: Which sentence is correct?
v.e: We use the -ed adjective for how a person feels: I'm interested in history. History is interesting.

v.q: It's ___ (embarrass) when you forget someone's name.
v.e: The situation causes the feeling, so we use the -ing adjective: embarrassing.

v.q: She was ___ (disappoint) with her exam results.
v.e: She is describing how she felt, so we use the -ed adjective: disappointed.

v.q: Something that makes you feel uncomfortable or silly is ___.
v.e: The cause: -ing.

v.q: I'm ___ by people who talk in the cinema.
v.e: How I feel: -ed.

v.q: Spiders really ___ me. I hate them.
v.e: Verb: scare me.

v.q: The ending of the film was very ___. I cried.
v.e: The cause of the feeling: moving.

v.q: I was so a___ when I lost my phone. (annoyed)
v.e: How I feel: annoyed.

v.q: The news was really s___ (shock). Nobody expected it.
v.e: The cause: shocking.

s: I wish I had studied harder for my English exam.
If only it would stop raining so we could go to the beach.
The ending of the film was really surprising.
I was so embarrassed when I fell over in front of everyone.

g.q: When I was a child, I ___ go to the beach every Sunday.
g.e: Used to + infinitive describes past habits that are no longer true.

g.q: I've lived in England for years, so I'm used to ___ on the left.
g.e: Be used to means be accustomed to. It is followed by a noun or -ing form: I'm used to driving.

g.q: It took me months to ___ used to the cold weather.
g.e: Get used to describes the process of becoming accustomed to something new.

g.q: Did you ___ have long hair?
g.e: In questions and negatives with did, we write use to (without -d): Did you use to...?

g.q: I ___ (not / use to) like vegetables, but now I love them.
g.e: The negative of used to is didn't use to (no -d after didn't).

g.q: My new job starts at six. I'm slowly getting used to ___ (get) up early.
g.e: After get used to we use the -ing form: getting used to getting up.

g.q: I ___ getting up early because I work in a bakery.
g.e: Be used to + -ing = be accustomed to.

g.q: We ___ live in Milan, but now we live in Palermo.
g.e: Past habit or state: used to + base verb.

g.q: You'll soon ___ driving on the left.
g.e: Get used to = become accustomed.

g.q: I'm not used to ___ so much.
g.e: Be used to + -ing.

g.q: When I moved to London, I had to get used to ___ on the left.
g.e: Get used to + -ing.

g.q: Did you ___ (use to) wear glasses?
g.e: Questions: did you use to...?

v.q: I ___ this morning and was late for school.
v.e: To oversleep means to sleep longer than you planned.

v.q: My dad ___ so loudly that nobody can sleep.
v.e: To snore means to make a loud noise while you are sleeping.

v.q: A short sleep during the day is a ___.
v.e: A nap is a short sleep, often after lunch. In Sicily many people have one in summer!

v.q: Feeling very tired after flying to a different time zone is called ___.
v.e: Jet lag is the tiredness you feel after a long flight across different time zones.

v.q: When you regularly can't sleep, you suffer from i___.
v.e: Insomnia is when you can't sleep, or can't sleep well.

v.q: A very bad, frightening dream: a n___
v.e: A nightmare is a frightening dream.

v.q: To sleep for a short time during the day: to have a ___.
v.e: Nap = short sleep.

v.q: If you can't sleep, you lie awake ___.
v.e: Toss and turn = move around in bed because you can't sleep.

v.q: A person who walks in their sleep is a ___.
v.e: Sleepwalker.

v.q: To set the time for your phone to wake you up: set the ___.
v.e: Set the alarm.

v.q: To go to sleep easily: to f___ asleep.
v.e: Fall asleep.

v.q: To sleep longer than you planned: to o___.
v.e: Oversleep.

s: I used to go to bed very late when I was a student.
I'm not used to getting up so early in the morning.
My brother snores so loudly that I can't fall asleep.
After a long flight, it takes a few days to get over jet lag.

g.q: I really enjoy ___ to jazz.
g.e: After enjoy we use the -ing form: I enjoy listening.

g.q: She decided ___ the piano.
g.e: After decide we use to + infinitive: she decided to learn.

g.q: I'll never forget ___ my favourite band live for the first time.
g.e: Forget + -ing refers to a memory of something you did in the past.

g.q: I'm thinking of ___ a band with my friends.
g.e: After a preposition (of) we always use the -ing form: thinking of starting.

g.q: Would you like ___ (come) to the concert with us?
g.e: After would like we use to + infinitive: would you like to come?

g.q: I can't stand ___ (wait) in long queues.
g.e: After can't stand we normally use the -ing form: I can't stand waiting.

g.q: I remember ___ my first concert. It was amazing.
g.e: Remember + -ing = a memory of the past.

g.q: Remember ___ the tickets!
g.e: Remember + to = don't forget to do something.

g.q: He stopped ___ the guitar when he was 20.
g.e: Stop + -ing = finish doing.

g.q: She avoids ___ in public.
g.e: Avoid + -ing.

g.q: I tried ___ (open) the window, but it was stuck.
g.e: Try to = make an effort.

g.q: It's worth ___ (listen) to this album.
g.e: It's worth + -ing.

v.q: The person who leads an orchestra is the ___.
v.e: The conductor stands in front of the orchestra and directs the musicians.

v.q: A group of people who sing together, for example in a church, is a ___.
v.e: A choir is a group of singers. An orchestra plays instruments.

v.q: The words of a song are the ___.
v.e: Lyrics are the words of a song. The tune is the music.

v.q: A song that is easy to remember is ___.
v.e: A catchy song has a tune that stays in your head.

v.q: Someone who writes music, like Verdi or Mozart: a c___
v.e: A composer writes music. A conductor directs the musicians.

v.q: A person who plays the drums: a d___
v.e: We often add -er to an instrument to name the player: drum - drummer.

v.q: A musician who plays alone, without a band: a ___ artist.
v.e: Solo artist.

v.q: A live music performance is a ___.
v.e: Gig (informal) = concert.

v.q: The part of a song that repeats is the ___.
v.e: Chorus.

v.q: A person who plays the violin is a ___.
v.e: Violinist.

v.q: One song on an album is a t___.
v.e: Track.

v.q: To sing or play music without preparation: to i___.
v.e: Improvise.

s: I'm thinking of learning to play the saxophone.
She's the lead singer in a band with her friends.
I can't stand listening to music that is too loud.
We decided to go to an outdoor concert in Palermo.

g.q: The lights are off. They ___ gone to bed.
g.e: Must have + past participle means we are almost sure something happened, because of the evidence.

g.q: She ___ seen me; she was looking the other way.
g.e: Can't have + past participle means we are sure something didn't happen.

g.q: I'd rather ___ at home tonight.
g.e: Would rather is followed by the infinitive without to: I'd rather stay.

g.q: You ___ told me it was your birthday! I'd have bought you a present.
g.e: Should have + past participle is used to criticise or show regret about the past.

g.q: I'd rather you ___ (not tell) anyone about this.
g.e: When would rather is followed by another person, we use the past simple: I'd rather you didn't tell...

g.q: I'm not sure where my keys are. I ___ (might / leave) them at school.
g.e: Might have + past participle means it's possible that something happened.

g.q: He ___ have left already. His coat is still here.
g.e: Can't have = sure it didn't happen.

g.q: You ___ have been so tired after the trip.
g.e: Must have = sure it happened.

g.q: I'm not sure. She ___ have missed the bus.
g.e: Might have = possible.

g.q: I'd rather ___ by train.
g.e: Would rather + base verb.

g.q: You ___ (should / tell) me you were ill! I would have helped.
g.e: Should have = criticism of a past action.

g.q: I'd rather you ___ (not / smoke) in the house.
g.e: Would rather + person + past simple.

v.q: Can you ___ me to buy some milk?
v.e: Remind someone to do something means help them not forget. Remember is what you do in your own head.

v.q: Could you ___ me your pen for a minute?
v.e: Lend = give something for a short time. Borrow = take something for a short time: Can I borrow your pen?

v.q: Prices ___ every year.
v.e: Rise has no object (prices rise). Raise needs an object (they raise prices).

v.q: The thieves ___ the bank last night.
v.e: You rob a person or a place. You steal a thing (they stole the money).

v.q: He refused to admit it. He d___ breaking the window.
v.e: Deny means say that you didn't do something. It is followed by -ing.

v.q: I didn't r___ that it was so late. We've missed the bus!
v.e: Realise means become aware of something, suddenly understand it.

v.q: Can you ___ my bag while I go to the toilet?
v.e: Watch = look after for a short time.

v.q: I can't ___ the noise any more!
v.e: Can't stand = can't tolerate.

v.q: The price of petrol has ___ again.
v.e: Rise (intransitive): prices rise. Raise needs an object.

v.q: Please ___ your hand if you have a question.
v.e: Raise + object: raise your hand.

v.q: I need to l___ down for a while. I'm tired.
v.e: Lie down (lie / lay / lain).

v.q: Don't forget to b___ your umbrella when you come. (to here)
v.e: Bring = to here. Take = to there.

s: You should have told me you were feeling ill.
She must have forgotten about our meeting this afternoon.
I'd rather stay at home than go out in this rain.
Could you lend me your dictionary until tomorrow?

g.q: This cake ___ delicious!
g.e: Verbs of the senses (taste, smell, look...) + adjective: it tastes delicious. We use like before a noun.

g.q: You ___ tired. Did you sleep well?
g.e: Look + adjective: you look tired. Look like is followed by a noun.

g.q: That ___ a great idea!
g.e: Sound like + noun phrase: that sounds like a great idea.

g.q: It looks ___ it's going to rain.
g.e: Look as if is followed by a clause (subject + verb): it looks as if it's going to rain.

g.q: This material ___ (feel) like silk.
g.e: Verbs of the senses are usually in the present simple, not the continuous: it feels like silk.

g.q: Your perfume smells ___ roses.
g.e: Smell like + noun or smell of + noun: it smells like/of roses.

g.q: She looks ___ she hasn't slept.
g.e: Look as if + clause.

g.q: This soup tastes ___.
g.e: Sense verbs + adjective.

g.q: He sounds ___ an American.
g.e: Sound like + noun.

g.q: I could hear someone ___ the piano.
g.e: Hear + object + -ing.

g.q: This bag feels ___ (lightly / light).
g.e: Sense verbs are followed by adjectives.

g.q: You look ___ your mother. (very similar)
g.e: Look like + noun.

v.q: You wear a ring on your ___.
v.e: A ring goes on your finger. A watch or bracelet goes on your wrist.

v.q: The joint in the middle of your arm is your ___.
v.e: Your elbow is where your arm bends. Your knee is where your leg bends.

v.q: When you close and open your eyes very quickly, you ___.
v.e: To blink is to close and open both eyes quickly.

v.q: When you move your head up and down to say yes, you ___.
v.e: We nod to say yes and shake our head to say no.

v.q: The top part of your leg, between your hip and your knee: t___
v.e: Your thigh is the top part of your leg, above your knee.

v.q: When you are very cold, your t___ chatter.
v.e: When you are very cold, your teeth chatter: they hit each other quickly.

v.q: To look at something for a long time: to ___.
v.e: Stare = look for a long time.

v.q: To look quickly at something: to ___.
v.e: Glance = a quick look.

v.q: To close one eye quickly as a signal: to ___.
v.e: Wink.

v.q: To move your shoulders up to say 'I don't know': to ___.
v.e: Shrug.

v.q: You use your t___ to taste food.
v.e: Tongue.

v.q: The joint between your hand and your arm: w___.
v.e: Wrist.

s: This soup smells wonderful and tastes even better.
You look as if you haven't slept for days.
She nodded and smiled, but she didn't say a word.
My shoulders and knees hurt after the long walk.

g.q: The thief ___ by the police yesterday.
g.e: With yesterday we use the past simple passive: was + past participle.

g.q: I ___ my hair cut last week.
g.e: Have something done means someone else does it for you: I had my hair cut (at the hairdresser's).

g.q: The robber is thought ___ the country.
g.e: He is thought to have + past participle talks about a past action that people believe happened.

g.q: It ___ that the painting is worth millions.
g.e: It is said that... is a passive structure for reporting what people say.

g.q: The new police station ___ (build) at the moment.
g.e: At the moment + passive: is being + past participle (present continuous passive).

g.q: My bike ___ (steal) last night.
g.e: Last night is finished past, so we use the past simple passive: was stolen.

g.q: I need to ___ my car repaired.
g.e: Have something done = someone else does it for you.

g.q: The painting ___ to be worth €2 million.
g.e: Passive reporting: is said to be.

g.q: The suspect is believed ___ the country last week.
g.e: Past action: to have + past participle.

g.q: The documents ___ by the police at the moment.
g.e: Present continuous passive.

g.q: We're ___ (have / the house / paint) next week.
g.e: Have + object + past participle.

g.q: It ___ (think) that the thief was a woman. Present passive.
g.e: It is thought that…

v.q: Someone who breaks into houses to steal things is a ___.
v.e: A burglar breaks into houses or buildings. A pickpocket steals from people's pockets or bags.

v.q: The jury found him ___ and he was sent to prison.
v.e: If you are guilty, you did the crime. Innocent means you didn't.

v.q: The judge gave her a ___ of two years in prison.
v.e: A sentence is the punishment a judge gives. The verdict is the jury's decision: guilty or not guilty.

v.q: Money that you have to pay as a punishment is a ___.
v.e: A fine is money you pay as a punishment, for example for parking in the wrong place.

v.q: Someone who sees a crime happen: a w___
v.e: A witness sees a crime and can tell the police or a court what happened.

v.q: The crime of damaging public property on purpose: v___
v.e: Vandalism is damaging property on purpose. The person is a vandal.

v.q: A person who steals from a shop is a ___.
v.e: Shoplifter.

v.q: Someone who illegally enters other people's computers is a ___.
v.e: Hacker.

v.q: To say officially that someone is responsible for a crime: to ___.
v.e: Charge someone with a crime.

v.q: When a court decides you didn't do it, you are found ___.
v.e: The verdict is 'not guilty'.

v.q: Taking someone and asking for money to free them: k___.
v.e: Kidnapping.

v.q: The person who decides the punishment in court: the j___.
v.e: Judge.

s: The museum was broken into and several paintings were stolen.
I'm having my car repaired at the garage this week.
The thief is believed to have escaped through the window.
The witness told the police exactly what she had seen.

g.q: She ___ me to call her later.
g.e: Tell + person + to + infinitive: she told me to call. We don't use say or suggest with this pattern.

g.q: He denied ___ the money.
g.e: Deny is followed by the -ing form: he denied taking the money.

g.q: My teacher advised me ___ more.
g.e: Advise + person + to + infinitive: she advised me to read more.

g.q: They suggested ___ to the beach.
g.e: Suggest is followed by -ing (or that + clause), never by an infinitive: they suggested going.

g.q: He apologised ___ (be) late.
g.e: Apologise for + -ing: he apologised for being late.

g.q: She refused ___ (answer) the journalist's questions.
g.e: Refuse is followed by to + infinitive: she refused to answer.

g.q: He ___ that he would never do it again.
g.e: Promise + that clause.

g.q: She accused me ___ her phone.
g.e: Accuse someone of + -ing.

g.q: They warned us ___ swim in the river.
g.e: Warn someone not to do something.

g.q: He admitted ___ the window.
g.e: Admit + -ing.

g.q: She ___ (insist) on paying for dinner.
g.e: Insist on + -ing.

g.q: My dad persuaded me ___ (study) law.
g.e: Persuade someone to do something.

v.q: A person who writes articles for a newspaper is a ___.
v.e: A journalist writes for newspapers or websites. A presenter introduces a TV or radio programme.

v.q: A newspaper with lots of celebrity gossip and big headlines is a ___.
v.e: A tabloid is a popular newspaper with short articles and gossip. Broadsheets are more serious.

v.q: Someone who writes reviews of films or books is a ___.
v.e: A critic gives their opinion about films, books, music or restaurants.

v.q: A report that only shows one side of the story is ___.
v.e: Biased means unfairly supporting one side. The opposite is objective.

v.q: The title of a newspaper article, in big letters: the h___
v.e: The headline is the title of a news story, usually printed in large letters.

v.q: Photographers who follow famous people to take photos of them: the p___
v.e: The paparazzi follow celebrities to take photos. One of them is a paparazzo.

v.q: The person in charge of a newspaper is the ___.
v.e: Editor.

v.q: A person who presents the news on TV: a news ___.
v.e: Presenter (newsreader).

v.q: A story that is not true but is shared as if it were: ___ news.
v.e: Fake news.

v.q: News that is happening right now: ___ news.
v.e: Breaking news.

v.q: Information that shows only one opinion is b___.
v.e: Biased = unfair, one-sided.

v.q: Someone who writes a regular column in a newspaper: a c___.
v.e: Columnist.

s: The journalist accused the politician of lying about the accident.
My friend persuaded me to start watching the news.
She admitted breaking the window and apologised to her neighbour.
I don't trust everything I read on social media.

g.q: ___ the rain, we went for a walk.
g.e: Despite is followed by a noun or -ing form: despite the rain. Although needs a clause (although it was raining).

g.q: I went to the bank ___ get some money.
g.e: We use to + infinitive to express purpose: I went to the bank to get money.

g.q: She got the job ___ she had no experience.
g.e: Even though is followed by a clause (subject + verb). Despite and in spite of need a noun or -ing form.

g.q: I'm saving money ___ I can buy a new bike.
g.e: So that is followed by a clause, often with can or will: so that I can buy.

g.q: In spite ___ being tired, she finished the race.
g.e: In spite of is always followed by a noun or -ing form: in spite of being tired.

g.q: Speak slowly so ___ everyone can understand you.
g.e: So that + clause expresses purpose: so that everyone can understand.

g.q: ___ she was tired, she kept working.
g.e: Although + clause.

g.q: ___ the cold, they went swimming.
g.e: Despite + noun.

g.q: I'm learning English ___ get a better job.
g.e: To + infinitive for purpose.

g.q: She whispered ___ not to wake the baby.
g.e: So as not to + infinitive.

g.q: He went to the gym ___ ___ ___ lose weight. (three words)
g.e: In order to + infinitive.

g.q: She passed ___ (despite / although) she didn't study.
g.e: Although + clause.

v.q: A short, memorable phrase used in advertising is a ___.
v.e: A slogan is a short, catchy phrase that people remember, used to advertise a product.

v.q: The ___ of a company is the design or symbol that it uses.
v.e: A logo is a symbol or design that represents a company.

v.q: When a company becomes bigger and opens new shops, it ___.
v.e: To expand means to become bigger. To set up means to start a business.

v.q: To start a new business means to ___ it.
v.e: To set up a business means to start it. To take over a company means to get control of it.

v.q: A person who buys goods or services: a c___
v.e: Customers (or consumers or clients) buy products or services from a business.

v.q: When a company introduces a new product, it l___ it.
v.e: To launch a product means to make it available to the public for the first time.

v.q: To pay to show your product on TV or online: to ___ it.
v.e: Advertise.

v.q: A company that makes money is making a ___.
v.e: Profit.

v.q: Two companies that join together ___.
v.e: Merge.

v.q: Another company that sells similar products is a ___.
v.e: Competitor.

v.q: A famous person in an advert who says a product is good gives an e___.
v.e: Endorsement.

v.q: To sell goods to other countries: to e___.
v.e: Export.

s: Although the advert was very funny, I didn't buy the product.
My uncle set up his own business in Palermo last year.
She works hard so that she can go on holiday in summer.
Despite the rain, lots of people came to the market.

g.q: Can you give me some ___ about the course?
g.e: Information is uncountable: it has no plural and we don't use a/an with it.

g.q: My trousers ___ too long.
g.e: Trousers is a plural noun (like jeans and scissors), so it takes a plural verb: are.

g.q: The news ___ very good today.
g.e: News looks plural but it is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb: the news is good.

g.q: We had ___ terrible weather on holiday.
g.e: Weather is uncountable, so we can't use a: such terrible weather.

g.q: She gave me some very good ___ (advise).
g.e: The noun is advice (uncountable). Advise is the verb.

g.q: Our luggage ___ (be) very heavy, so we took a taxi.
g.e: Luggage is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb: was/is.

g.q: The furniture ___ very old.
g.e: Furniture is uncountable: singular verb.

g.q: My jeans ___ dirty.
g.e: Jeans is plural: plural verb.

g.q: Can I give you ___ advice?
g.e: Advice is uncountable: a piece of advice.

g.q: The police ___ looking for him.
g.e: Police takes a plural verb.

g.q: Maths ___ (be) my favourite subject.
g.e: Maths is singular, even though it ends in -s.

g.q: I need some new ___ (furniture / furnitures).
g.e: Furniture never takes -s.

v.q: Someone who is not patient is ___.
v.e: We use the prefix im- before many adjectives starting with p: impatient, impossible, impolite.

v.q: To read something again is to ___ it.
v.e: The prefix re- means again: reread, rewrite, redo.

v.q: If you ___ someone, you understand them wrongly.
v.e: The prefix mis- means wrongly: misunderstand, mispronounce.

v.q: The adjective from 'danger' is ___.
v.e: The suffix -ous makes adjectives from nouns: danger - dangerous, fame - famous.

v.q: The noun from 'improve' is ___.
v.e: The suffix -ment makes nouns from verbs: improve - improvement, develop - development.

v.q: Not possible: ___ (possible)
v.e: We add the prefix im- to possible to make the opposite: impossible.

v.q: The opposite of 'honest' is ___.
v.e: Dis- + honest.

v.q: To do something again: ___.
v.e: Re- = again.

v.q: The company wants to ___ 20 new staff next year.
v.e: Take on = employ.

v.q: The noun from 'kind' is ___.
v.e: -ness forms nouns from adjectives.

v.q: Not legal: i___.
v.e: Il- + legal.

v.q: The noun from 'develop' is d___.
v.e: -ment.

s: The furniture in our new flat is really modern and comfortable.
Could you give me some advice about learning English?
Many people are unhappy about the traffic in the city centre.
My jeans are too small, so I need a new pair.

g.q: ___ of my parents are doctors.
g.e: We use both for two people or things: both of my parents are doctors.

g.q: ___ student has a laptop.
g.e: Every is followed by a singular noun: every student. All, both and most need a plural noun.

g.q: I've got two brothers, but ___ of them lives at home.
g.e: Neither means not one and not the other, for two people or things. None is for three or more.

g.q: There's ___ milk in the fridge. Can you buy some?
g.e: No + noun in a positive sentence means 'not any': there's no milk.

g.q: You can have e___ tea or coffee. Which would you prefer?
g.e: Either... or... is used to talk about a choice between two things.

g.q: N___ of the students passed the test; they all failed.
g.e: None of means not one of a group of three or more.

g.q: ___ my parents speak English.
g.e: Both = the two of them.

g.q: ___ of the two answers is correct. They're both wrong.
g.e: Neither = not one and not the other.

g.q: I've read ___ book in the library.
g.e: Every + singular noun.

g.q: ___ the students passed.
g.e: All (of) the + plural.

g.q: We can meet ___ Monday or Tuesday. (one of two)
g.e: Either… or…

g.q: ___ of us knows the answer. (not one person)
g.e: None of = not any.

v.q: A person who does experiments in a laboratory is a ___.
v.e: Scientist is the person. Science is the subject and scientific is the adjective.

v.q: Scientists carry ___ experiments to test their ideas.
v.e: We say carry out an experiment, meaning do it.

v.q: When a scientist finds something that nobody knew before, they make a ___.
v.e: You make a discovery when you find something that already existed. An invention is a new thing someone creates.

v.q: An idea that tries to explain something but has not been proved yet is a ___.
v.e: A theory is an explanation that scientists are still testing.

v.q: A room where scientists do experiments: a l___
v.e: A laboratory, or lab for short, is where scientists work.

v.q: Someone who creates a new machine or device: an i___
v.e: An inventor invents (creates) something new, like the telephone.

v.q: To show that something is true: to ___ it.
v.e: Prove.

v.q: Something that isn't harmful but is useful in medicine is ___.
v.e: Beneficial.

v.q: The animals or people tested in an experiment are the test ___.
v.e: Test subjects.

v.q: A medicine that kills bacteria: an ___.
v.e: Antibiotic.

v.q: A test in a laboratory: an e___.
v.e: Experiment.

v.q: Something new and important that is achieved: a b___.
v.e: Breakthrough.

s: Both of my sisters want to become scientists.
Every student in the class carried out an experiment.
Neither of the theories has been proved yet.
Scientists have made an amazing discovery about the ocean.

g.q: ___ is full of surprises.
g.e: We don't use the with abstract nouns when we talk about them in general: life, love, happiness.

g.q: My sister is ___ engineer, and she loves her job.
g.e: We use a/an with jobs. Engineer starts with a vowel sound, so we use an.

g.q: We went to ___ Canary Islands last summer.
g.e: We use the with groups of islands and plural countries: the Canary Islands, the United States.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
g.e: We don't use the when we talk about things in general: I love Italian food.

g.q: What ___ amazing view!
g.e: What + a/an + singular noun is used in exclamations. Amazing starts with a vowel sound, so we use an.

g.q: Can you pass me ___ salt, please?
g.e: We use the when both people know which one we mean: the salt on the table.

g.q: ___ is very important for children.
g.e: General abstract noun: no article.

g.q: ___ Alps are beautiful in winter.
g.e: Mountain ranges take the.

g.q: He's in ___ hospital. (as a patient)
g.e: In hospital (as a patient): no article in BrE.

g.q: She plays ___ tennis every Saturday.
g.e: Sports: no article.

g.q: We visited ___ United States last year.
g.e: Countries with 'States', 'Kingdom'… take the.

g.q: ___ Mount Etna is a volcano.
g.e: Single mountains take no article.

v.q: I just want some peace and ___.
v.e: Peace and quiet is a fixed word pair meaning a calm situation with no noise.

v.q: Let's think about the pros and ___ before we decide.
v.e: Pros and cons are the advantages and disadvantages of something.

v.q: Every relationship has its ups and ___.
v.e: Ups and downs are the good and bad times. The word order is fixed.

v.q: Don't worry, she'll find out sooner or ___.
v.e: Sooner or later means at some time in the future, although we don't know when.

v.q: The children arrived home safe and s___ after the school trip.
v.e: Safe and sound means safe and not hurt.

v.q: We don't go to the cinema often, just now and t___.
v.e: Now and then means sometimes, but not often.

v.q: We need to wait for the dust to ___ (= wait until things calm down).
v.e: Let the dust settle.

v.q: Let's sort out the ___ and ends before we leave.
v.e: Odds and ends = small things.

v.q: I'm sick and ___ of this rain!
v.e: Sick and tired of = very annoyed by.

v.q: The rules are black and ___: no phones in class.
v.e: Black and white = very clear.

v.q: We've had lots of ups and d___ this year.
v.e: Ups and downs.

v.q: Learning a language takes time, but step by s___ you improve.
v.e: Step by step.

s: I love the peace and quiet of the countryside.
We discussed the pros and cons of living in a big city.
The sun was shining and the sea was really calm.
Sooner or later, everyone makes a mistake in life.
